newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco shares stumble amid more settlement talk. [CORRECTED 21:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Tobacco shares stumble amid more settlement talk. [CORRECTED 21:05 GMT]

text.p: Tobacco stocks were mostly lower Friday amid profit-taking after a string of recent winning sessions, but behind the scenes the talk was of a quantum shift in the industry's approach toward its foes.

Comments made December 5 by Steven Goldstone, chairman and chief executive of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, point to the growing likelihood that the tobacco industry would accede to mass settlement terms and government oversight, if the terms were right.

Parts of Goldstone's speech at Northeastern University in Boston, quoted in the December 23 editions of Business Week Magazine, extend allusions Goldstone made in March that he would favor a settlement pact with the government.
Goldstone said "a lot of forces are at work" favoring some broad settlement with industry adversaries. (Corrects sense of comments.)
"In 1997, the most meaningful thing I can do is come to some solution on this problem," Business Week quotes him a saying.

Industry analysts said the most liketly settlement would allow the industry to fight current suits but protect itself from future litigation by agreeing to fund a multibillion-dollar pool for victims.
That would come from a tax on cigarettes of anywhere from $0.20 to $0.35 per pack.
Lawyers for RJR said the company had not backed off from plans to fight the suits.

The magazine article came on the heels of a report issued by Gary Black, a leading tobacco industry analyst with Sanford C. Bernstein. Black wrote that some within the industry had undergone a "180-degree turn in attitude" toward the idea of agreeing to settle.

Black's firm owns large chunks of tobacco shares, and Black himself was reported to have been offered a position on the slate that has been proposed by dissident shareholders to oust the current board of RJR Nabisco.
The groundswell of settlement rumors came ironically amid legal developments in Massachussets and Florida on Friday.

In West Palm Beach, Fla., a county circuit judge denied a motion by tobacco companies to stop the state from suing the industry using state racketeering laws as part of the state's effort to reclaim expenses in the treatment of tobacco illnesses.
If the state won, the court could triple the $1 billion in damages currently sought in the suit.
In Massachussets, tobacco companies argued that a proposed state law requiring cigarette packages to include a label listing ingredients would compromise trade secrets.
The new law would take effect July 1.

Eighteen states and several big cities have launched massive suits against tobacco companies for the recovery of state Medicaid expenses. Also peppering the industry are scattered personal-injury suits and other state class-action suits.

Shares in Philip Morris Cos Inc were down 2-3/8 at 111-1/2 in late trading after posting a new 52-week high of 119 earlier in the week. Stock in RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, the parent company of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, was down 3/4 at 32-3/4. Smaller tobacco company shares were 5/8 lower to 1/8 firmer.
